definition: To firmly reject something and refuse to accept it or be linked with it.
example: Years later, the scientist repudiated her early theory once new data showed it could not be right.
nuance: To repudiate is to reject or disown something, while to refute is to prove it false with evidence.
prompt: A chess club realizes that a bylaw it wrote long ago was unfair to beginners.
options: The club voted to repudiate the old bylaw and publicly apologized to the beginners it had excluded.
The club voted to repudiate the old bylaw so that its rules would be enforced even more strictly.
Each member was asked to repudiate the bylaw aloud twice so that everyone would memorize its wording.
Proud of the bylaw's fairness, the members chose to repudiate it by framing it above the front door.
reasons: Formally rejecting an unfair rule and taking responsibility for it fits the word exactly.
Rejecting a rule cannot also mean making it stronger, so this reverses the meaning.
This treats the word like "repeat" or "recite," a sound-alike confusion.
Displaying a rule with pride honors it; the word requires turning away from it.

practice.prompt: A novelist learns that a made-up interview with her is being passed around online.
options: The novelist moved quickly to repudiate the interview, noting that she had never met the reporter.
The novelist decided to repudiate the interview by proudly sharing it with every one of her readers.
The novelist hoped to repudiate her good name by winning a second major literary prize this year.
The novelist chose to repudiate the interview by adding it to the official list of her published works.
reasons: Publicly denying any connection to a false interview is a clear act of disowning it.
Spreading something proudly is endorsing it, not rejecting it.
This confuses the word with "repute"; winning prizes builds a reputation rather than rejecting anything.
Claiming the interview as her own work is the opposite of refusing to be linked with it.
